theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: R-L, R-C and R-L-C Circuits

Complex (j) notation turns phasor diagrams into ordinary algebra. A resistor has impedance R, an inductor +jX_L and a capacitor −jX_C, so a series circuit has Z = R + j(X_L − X_C). The magnitude |Z| gives the current from I = V/|Z|, and the angle φ = tan⁻¹((X_L − X_C)/R) tells you whether the current lags (positive φ) or leads (negative φ). Multiplying every side of the impedance triangle by I gives the voltage triangle V_R, V_X and V, which is why voltmeter readings in a series circuit never add arithmetically.

theoryAdd.plainText: Z = R + j(XL − XC) = |Z| at angle φ; I = V / |Z|

theoryAdd.text: In a parallel circuit the voltage is common and the branch currents add as phasors. The resistor current I_R = V/R is in phase with V, the inductor current I_L = V/X_L lags by 90° and the capacitor current I_C = V/X_C leads by 90°, so I_L and I_C partly cancel. The total current is √(I_R² + (I_C − I_L)²) and the combined impedance is V divided by that current, always smaller than the smallest branch opposition in an R-L or R-C pair.

theoryAdd.latex: I = \sqrt{I_R^2 + (I_C - I_L)^2}, \qquad Z_{R\parallel X} = \frac{R X}{\sqrt{R^2 + X^2}}
theoryAdd.plainText: I = √(I_R² + (I_C − I_L)²); R in parallel with X: Z = RX / √(R² + X²)

rows: Raising f in an R-L pair

theoryAdd.text: The transient results come from one first-order equation. For an R-L circuit, KVL gives V = Ri + L di/dt, whose solution rising from zero is i = (V/R)(1 − e^(−Rt/L)); the R-C case is identical with v_C in place of i and RC in place of L/R. Two continuity rules fix the starting point: capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot jump. So at t = 0+ an uncharged capacitor acts as a short circuit and an inductor carrying no initial current as an open circuit, while in DC steady state the capacitor is open and the inductor is a short. The time to reach any voltage v on a rising curve follows by taking logarithms.

theoryAdd.plainText: t = τ ln(V / (V − v)); time to 50 % = 0.693 τ

theoryAdd.text:
Example 1: series R = 15 Ω, L = 0.2 H, C = 80 µF on 230 V, 50 Hz
X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.2 = 62.83 Ω
X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 80×10⁻⁶) = 39.79 Ω
Net X = 62.83 − 39.79 = 23.04 Ω (inductive)
|Z| = √(15² + 23.04²) = 27.50 Ω
I = 230/27.50 = 8.37 A, lagging by φ = tan⁻¹(23.04/15) = 56.9°
Power factor = cos φ = 15/27.50 = 0.546 lagging
V_R = 125.5 V, V_L = 525.6 V, V_C = 332.8 V
Note V_L = 526 V exceeds the 230 V supply; check √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²) = 230 V

Example 2: R = 47 kΩ, C = 22 µF (uncharged) switched onto 12 V DC
τ = RC = 47×10³ × 22×10⁻⁶ = 1.034 s
Initial current i(0+) = V/R = 12/47 kΩ = 0.255 mA (capacitor acts as a short)
At t = 1 s: v_C = 12(1 − e^(−1/1.034)) = 7.44 V
Time to reach 9 V: t = τ ln(12/(12 − 9)) = 1.034 × ln 4 = 1.43 s
Practically fully charged after 5τ = 5.2 s
Common mistakes and how to avoid them:
items: Adding V_R + V_L + V_C, or R + X, arithmetically; use the square root of squares because they are 90° apart.
Forgetting to convert mH to H and µF to F before using 2πfL or 1/(2πfC).
Assuming X_L > X_C always means lagging current; that is true in series, but in parallel the larger current flows in the smaller reactance, so X_L > X_C makes a parallel circuit capacitive.
Using τ = R/L or τ = RL for an R-L circuit; the correct time constant is L/R.
Treating a capacitor as an open circuit at the switching instant; it is a short at t = 0+ and an open circuit only in DC steady state.

theoryAdd.text: For any series circuit question, write X_L, X_C, net X, |Z|, I and φ in that order before looking at the options. Most wrong options come from skipping the net-reactance step or from adding R and X directly.

questions.questionText: What is the reactance of a 50 mH inductor at 50 Hz?
questions.explanation: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.05 = 15.71 Ω. Using 50 instead of 0.05 H gives 15708 Ω, a unit slip.

questions.questionText: A 10 µF capacitor is connected to a 50 Hz supply. Its capacitive reactance is:
questions.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 10×10⁻⁶) = 318.3 Ω. 0.00314 Ω is 2πfC, the reciprocal mistake.

questions.questionText: If the supply frequency applied to a capacitor is doubled, its capacitive reactance:
questions.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) is inversely proportional to frequency, so doubling f halves X_C.

questions.questionText: The reciprocal of the impedance of an AC circuit is called its:
questions.explanation: Y = 1/Z = G + jB, measured in siemens; its real part is the conductance G and its imaginary part is the susceptance B. Admittances of parallel branches add directly.

questions.questionText: A capacitor charges from 0 V through a resistor from a DC source. What percentage of the final voltage has it reached after one time constant?
questions.explanation: v_C/V = 1 − e^(−1) = 1 − 0.368 = 0.632, i.e. 63.2 %. 36.8 % is what remains of a decaying quantity, and 86.5 % is reached after 2τ.

questions.questionText: What is the time constant of a series circuit with R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 µF?
A coil of inductance 0.5 H and resistance 10 Ω is switched onto a DC supply. What is its time constant?
questions.explanation: τ = L/R = 0.5/10 = 0.05 s = 50 ms. 5 s is L × R and 20 s is R/L.

questions.questionText: In the phasor diagram of a series R-L circuit, the voltage across the resistor is:
options: 180° out of phase with the current
questions.explanation: A resistor's voltage V_R = IR is always in phase with its current; only the inductor voltage leads the current by 90°.

questions.questionText: Which quantity is the same for every element of a series R-L-C circuit?
questions.explanation: Series elements carry the same current; their voltages differ in size and phase. In a parallel circuit it is the voltage that is common.

questions.questionText: A series circuit has R = 5 Ω and X_C = 12 Ω. What is the magnitude of its impedance?
questions.explanation: |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 Ω. 17 Ω is the arithmetic sum, a common error.

questions.questionText: In a series R-L circuit the voltmeter readings are V_R = 30 V and V_L = 40 V. What is the supply voltage?
questions.explanation: V_R and V_L are 90° apart, so V = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V, not the arithmetic sum of 70 V.

questions.questionText: What is the smallest whole number of time constants after which an R-C or R-L transient has completed more than 99 % of its total change?
questions.explanation: 1 − e^(−n): 3τ gives 95.0 %, 4τ gives 98.2 % and 5τ gives 99.3 %, so five time constants are needed.

questions.questionText: A series circuit of R = 40 Ω and L = 0.1 H is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz. What current flows?
A series R-C circuit has R = 10 Ω and X_C = 10 Ω. The phase angle between the supply voltage and the current is:
questions.explanation: tan φ = X_C/R = 10/10 = 1, so φ = 45°. In an R-C circuit the current leads the voltage.

questions.questionText: A series R-C circuit has R = 24 Ω and X_C = 7 Ω. Its power factor is:
questions.explanation: |Z| = √(24² + 7²) = 25 Ω and pf = R/|Z| = 24/25 = 0.96, leading because the circuit is capacitive. 0.28 is X_C/|Z| (sin φ).

questions.questionText: A series R-L-C circuit has R = 8 Ω, X_L = 20 Ω and X_C = 14 Ω. Its impedance and phase angle are:
questions.explanation: Net X = 20 − 14 = 6 Ω (inductive), |Z| = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω and φ = tan⁻¹(6/8) = 36.9°, current lagging.

questions.questionText: In a series R-L-C circuit, V_R = 60 V, V_L = 120 V and V_C = 40 V. What is the supply voltage?
questions.explanation: V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²) = √(60² + 80²) = 100 V. 220 V is the arithmetic sum.

questions.questionText: In a series R-L-C circuit, X_C is greater than X_L. The circuit behaves as:
options: Capacitive, with the current leading the supply voltage
Inductive, with the current lagging the supply voltage
Purely resistive, with the current in phase
An open circuit, with zero current
questions.explanation: The net reactance X_L − X_C is negative (capacitive), so the current leads the supply voltage by tan⁻¹((X_C − X_L)/R).

questions.questionText: Which statement about a series R-L-C circuit on AC is correct?
options: The supply voltage is the arithmetic sum V_R + V_L + V_C
V_L and V_C are in phase with each other
The current is always in phase with the supply voltage
The voltage across L or C alone can be greater than the supply voltage
questions.explanation: V_L and V_C are 180° apart and partly cancel, so each can exceed the supply voltage while their difference stays small.

questions.questionText: A capacitor charges from 0 V through a resistor from a 10 V DC supply with a time constant of 1 ms. What is the capacitor voltage 2 ms after switching on?
questions.explanation: v_C = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)) = 10(1 − e^(−2)) = 10(1 − 0.135) = 8.65 V. 1.35 V is the remaining difference, not the capacitor voltage.

questions.questionText: A capacitor charged to 100 V discharges through a resistor with a time constant of 2 s. What is its voltage 2 s after discharge begins?
questions.explanation: v = V₀e^(−t/τ) = 100 e^(−1) = 36.8 V. After one time constant a decaying quantity keeps 36.8 % of its initial value.

questions.questionText: A 12 V DC supply is switched onto a coil with R = 4 Ω and L = 2 H. What is the current 0.5 s after switching?
An uncharged capacitor in series with a 5 kΩ resistor is switched onto a 20 V DC supply. What current flows at the instant of switching (t = 0+)?
questions.explanation: An uncharged capacitor cannot change its voltage instantly, so it acts as a short at t = 0+: i = V/R = 20/5000 = 4 mA. The current then decays exponentially.

questions.questionText: At the instant a DC source is switched onto a series R-L circuit whose inductor carries no initial current, the inductor behaves as:
options: A short circuit, so the initial current is V/R
An open circuit, so the initial current is zero
questions.explanation: Inductor current cannot change instantaneously, so it starts at zero; the whole supply voltage appears across L at t = 0+.

questions.questionText: At what frequency does a 20 mH inductor have a reactance of 100 Ω?
questions.explanation: f = X_L/(2πL) = 100/(2π × 0.02) = 795.8 Hz. 5000 is X_L/L, which is ω in rad/s, not f in Hz.

questions.questionText: A 30 Ω resistor and an inductor of reactance 40 Ω are connected in parallel across 120 V AC. What is the total supply current?
questions.explanation: I_R = 120/30 = 4 A and I_L = 120/40 = 3 A, 90° apart, so I = √(4² + 3²) = 5 A. 2.4 A would be the series-circuit answer 120/50.

questions.questionText: A 30 Ω resistor is connected in parallel with a capacitor of reactance 40 Ω. What is the magnitude of the combined impedance?
questions.explanation: |Z| = RX_C/√(R² + X_C²) = 30 × 40/50 = 24 Ω. 17.1 Ω is the product-over-sum formula applied as if both were resistors.

questions.questionText: A resistor and a capacitor are connected in parallel across an AC supply. Which statement is correct?
options: The supply current lags the voltage
The supply current leads the voltage and |Z| is smaller than R
The supply current equals the arithmetic sum of the branch currents
|Z| is larger than both R and X_C
questions.explanation: The capacitor branch current leads V by 90°, pulling the total current ahead of V. Branch currents add as phasors, and a parallel combination is always smaller than either branch.

questions.questionText: A 10 Ω resistor in series with a capacitive reactance of 5 Ω has an impedance, in rectangular form, of:
questions.explanation: Capacitive reactance is written as −jX_C, so Z = 10 − j5 Ω, with magnitude √125 = 11.2 Ω.

questions.questionText: A series R-C circuit with R = 60 Ω and X_C = 80 Ω is connected to 100 V AC. What is the voltage across the capacitor?
questions.explanation: |Z| = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω, I = 100/100 = 1 A and V_C = IX_C = 80 V. 57.1 V comes from treating the circuit as a resistive divider.

questions.questionText: Which quantity cannot change instantaneously at a switching instant (finite voltages and currents assumed)?
questions.explanation: Changing v_C instantly would need infinite current (i = C dv/dt). The inductor's current, not its voltage, is the other continuous quantity.

questions.questionText: In a series R-L circuit with fixed R and L, the supply frequency is increased at constant voltage. Which change occurs?
options: The impedance rises, the current falls and the lagging phase angle increases
The impedance falls, the current rises and the phase angle decreases
The impedance and phase angle stay the same
The current begins to lead the voltage
questions.explanation: X_L = 2πfL grows with f, so |Z| = √(R² + X_L²) rises, I = V/|Z| falls and φ = tan⁻¹(X_L/R) increases towards 90° lagging.

questions.questionText: Which statement about reactance is NOT correct?
options: Inductive reactance is proportional to frequency
Capacitive reactance is inversely proportional to frequency
An ideal reactance dissipates average power just as a resistance does
questions.explanation: An ideal inductor or capacitor stores energy for part of each cycle and returns it, so its average power is zero. The other statements are true.

questions.questionText: A series circuit of R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 50 µF is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz. The current and its phase relation to the supply voltage are:
A coil draws 5 A from a 100 V DC supply and 4 A from a 100 V, 50 Hz AC supply. What is its inductance?
questions.explanation: DC gives R = 100/5 = 20 Ω; AC gives |Z| = 100/4 = 25 Ω, so X_L = √(25² − 20²) = 15 Ω and L = 15/(2π × 50) = 47.7 mH. 79.6 mH wrongly uses |Z| as X_L.

questions.questionText: A 1 µF capacitor, initially uncharged, charges through a 1 MΩ resistor from a 10 V DC supply. How long does it take to reach 5 V?
questions.explanation: τ = RC = 10⁶ × 10⁻⁶ = 1 s. From 5 = 10(1 − e^(−t/τ)), e^(−t) = 0.5 and t = τ ln 2 = 0.693 s. One τ (1 s) would give 6.32 V.

questions.questionText: A 20 V DC supply is switched onto a coil with R = 5 Ω and L = 0.4 H. In steady state, the current and the energy stored in the magnetic field are:
questions.explanation: Steady-state current I = V/R = 20/5 = 4 A (the inductor is a short). Stored energy W = ½LI² = 0.5 × 0.4 × 4² = 3.2 J; 6.4 J forgets the ½.

questions.questionText: A series R-C circuit with R = 40 Ω draws 4 A from a 200 V, 50 Hz supply. What is the capacitance?
A series R-L-C circuit has R = 20 Ω, X_L = 50 Ω and X_C = 35 Ω and carries 4 A. What are the supply voltage and the voltage across the inductor?
questions.explanation: |Z| = √(20² + 15²) = 25 Ω, so V = 4 × 25 = 100 V, while V_L = IX_L = 4 × 50 = 200 V. The inductor voltage exceeds the supply because V_C (140 V) opposes it.

questions.questionText: A 40 Ω resistor, an inductor of reactance 30 Ω and a capacitor of reactance 60 Ω are connected in parallel across 120 V AC. The supply current is:
questions.explanation: I_R = 3 A, I_L = 4 A (lagging), I_C = 2 A (leading); I = √(3² + (4 − 2)²) = √13 = 3.61 A. The inductive branch current is larger, so the total lags.

questions.questionText: A 100 µF capacitor, initially uncharged, is charged through 10 kΩ from a 50 V DC supply. What is the charging current 1 s after switching on?
questions.explanation: τ = RC = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁴ = 1 s and i(0+) = 50/10⁴ = 5 mA, so i = 5e^(−1) = 1.84 mA. 3.16 mA wrongly uses the rising factor (1 − e^(−1)).

questions.questionText: A series R-L circuit has R = 100 Ω and L = 0.1 H. At what supply frequency does the current lag the voltage by exactly 45°?
questions.explanation: φ = 45° requires X_L = R = 100 Ω, so f = R/(2πL) = 100/(2π × 0.1) = 159.2 Hz. 1000 is ω = R/L in rad/s.
